GLOSSARY
CIDP = chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy; ITB = intrathecal baclofen; SPS = stiff 
person syndrome
S
tiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare, neuroimmunolog-
ical disorder that results in progressive but fluctuating 
muscular rigidity, spasms, and cocontraction of agonist 
and antagonist muscles. SPS results from decreased synthe-
sis of γ-aminobutyric acid through autoantibodies to glu-
tamic acid decarboxylase and is often associated with other 
autoimmune diseases. The presence of these antibodies in 
the setting of clinical symptoms is highly suggestive of SPS. 
First-line treatments for SPS include corticosteroids, plas-
mapheresis, and intravenous immunoglobulin and dimin-
ish the immune response. Second-line immunomodulators 
include rituximab, cyclophosphamide, and mycophenolate, 
but elevate the risk of infections.
1 If the spasms are painful or 
functionally limiting, treatment includes benzodiazepines, 
anticonvulsants, baclofen, tizanidine, or botulinum toxin 
injections. In later stages, SPS can result in spinal deformi-
ties such as cervical or lumbar lordosis. However, there are 
no reports of scoliosis associated with SPS and a report of 
scoliosis in childhood-onset SPS.
2 Progression of SPS leads 
to frequent falls, anxiety, depression, and impaired mobility 
and activities of daily living.
3
Severe spasticity and spasms, pronounced in the bilateral 
lower extremities, can be treated with intrathecal baclofen, 
delivered by a pump. Specifically, this is a viable option 
when tone is functionally limiting, intractably painful, or 
refractory to oral antispasmodics and/or injectable medica-
tions such as botulinum toxin. Baclofen reduces tone and 
spasms and improves perceived comfort as well as function. 
Side effects include constipation, lethargy, confusion, hypo-
tonia, catheter-related complications, and pump malfunc-
tions that can lead to baclofen overdose or withdrawal. Many 
of these adverse effects have been reported in patients with 
SPS. Nevertheless, intrathecal baclofen is a viable option to 
improve tone and ambulation for SPS that is refractory to 
conservative measures.
4–6 One less well-characterized side 
effect is accelerated progression of underlying neuromus-
cular scoliosis. This has been described in pediatric patients 
with cerebral palsy.
7–11 However, there are no reported cases 
of accelerated scoliosis in an adult patient with neuromuscu-
lar disease such as SPS. In this report, we describe the accel-
erated progression of scoliosis after initiation of intrathecal 
baclofen in an adult with SPS and underlying thoracolum-
bar scoliotic curvature. This article adheres to the Enhancing 
the QUAlity and Transparency Of health Research guideline. 
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act autho-
rization was obtained from the patient.
CASE PRESENTATION AND RESULTS
This is a 59-year-old woman with chronic inflammatory 
demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP), SPS, and underly-
ing stable thoracolumbar scoliotic curvature (patient had 
this since childhood), who initially presented to us with 
functional deterioration from SPS with intractable muscle

spasms in the bilateral lower extremities, low back, and 
right upper extremity. In regard to her CIDP , her symp-
toms were burning paresthesias in her fingers and toes with 
associated gait instability, but no axial weakness, hyper -
tonia, or spasms, which are consistent with CIDP’s predi-
lection for lower motor neurons. She was diagnosed with 
CIDP via electrodiagnostic studies, completed intravenous 
Stiff person syndrome is a neuroimmunological disorder characterized by progressive muscu-
lar rigidity and spasms that affect axial/limb muscles, resulting in severe pain and functional 
limitations. When refractory to conservative treatments, intrathecal baclofen is a viable 
option to treat the increased tone. Intrathecal baclofen has been shown to accelerate under-
lying neuromuscular scoliosis in the pediatric population with cerebral palsy. This adverse 
effect has never been reported in adults with stiff person syndrome. We report a case of 
an adult with stiff person syndrome and underlying scoliosis who experienced accelerated 
progression of scoliosis after initiation of intrathecal baclofen, subsequently requiring neuro-
surgical intervention.  (A&A Practice. 2020;14:e01204.)

immunoglobulin (before SPS diagnosis), and was main-
tained on gabapentin and pregabalin with improvement 
of associated neuropathic pain. Two years after her CIDP 
diagnosis, she was diagnosed with SPS, given newly fluc-
tuating muscle rigidity and antiglutamic acid decarboxyl-
ase antibodies. Notably, thyroid function tests, vitamin B
12, 
and folate levels were unremarkable. Antibodies against 
human T-lymphotropic virus-1, amphiphysin, and pan-
creatic islet cells as well as paraneoplastic antibodies were 
negative. For 4 years following her diagnosis, she trialed 
multiple medications to manage her spasms and tone. 
Unfortunately, her severe spasms were recalcitrant to 
oral baclofen, tizanidine, and diazepam. Additionally, the 
patient received intravenous immunoglobulin again, which 
gave temporary relief but resulted in severe headaches and 
fatigue. Plasmapheresis resulted in faintness and dizzi-
ness. Intravenous methylprednisolone and oral prednisone 
resulted in epistaxis. She underwent an intrathecal baclofen 
trial that resulted in improved spasms and pain. As such, 
a pump was placed with the catheter tip at the T10 level 
as confirmed by fluoroscopy, 4 years after her initial diag-
nosis of SPS. The patient’s intrathecal baclofen dosage was 
uptitrated against functional and pain improvements, from 
baclofen 100 µg per day on pump implantation to baclofen 
475.1 µg per day over the next 5 years. Notably, although she 
had been taking oral baclofen 10 mg every 6 hours, tizani-
dine 6 mg every 8 hours, and diazepam 5 mg every 6 hours 
as needed at the beginning of intrathecal baclofen therapy, 
she was able to gradually wean off all oral antispasmodics. 
Over the 5 years following intrathecal baclofen initiation, 
the patient had reduced spasms and returned to function/
ambulation with dose titration.
However, over these 5 years, the patient had gradu-
ally increasing low back pain and worsening gait instabil-
ity. When she presented to us, the patient’s right inferior 
rib was nearly in contact with her iliac crest and she was 
having significant difficulty with mobility and her activi-
ties of daily living. Before and after intrathecal baclofen 
initiation, radiography demonstrated a progression of tho-
racic dextroscoliosis with a Cobb angle of 40° (from 10°, 5 
years prior) and lumbar levoscoliosis with a Cobb angle of 
50° (from 8°, 5 years prior; see Figures 1 and 2). Her radio-
graph also revealed a left lateral listhesis of L4 on L5 and L3 
on L4 as well as grade 1 retrolisthesis of L3–4 and grade 1 
anterolisthesis of L4–5. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry 
showed low bone density. Neurosurgical intervention with 
L4-S1 anterior lumbar interbody fusion and T10 to iliac 
posterior fusion with osteotomies resulted in functional 
improvement.
DISCUSSION
This case report demonstrates that intrathecal baclofen 
may contribute to accelerated scoliotic progression in 
patients with underlying scoliotic curvature and SPS. 
Baclofen counteracts the γ -aminobutyric acid deficit in 
SPS through agonism and often improves spasticity, 
function, and pain. Our patient’s spasms and spastic-
ity were well controlled on intrathecal baclofen and she

experienced functional gain. However, her underlying 
thoracolumbar scoliotic curvature (stable since childhood) 
rapidly developed into severe scoliosis, coinciding with 
intrathecal baclofen initiation, ultimately requiring sur -
gery. While the mechanism of scoliotic acceleration with 
intrathecal baclofen is not well understood, it is feasible 
that the approach unequally deposits baclofen such that 
there is lateralization of medication. This may accelerate 
scoliotic progression by asymmetrically reducing axial 
muscle tone, unmasking weakness, and impairing muscle 
coordination.
11 The effect of intrathecal baclofen on sco-
liosis is further accelerated in patients with underlying 
neuromuscular disease such as SPS, in which patients are 
often unable to ambulate for long periods, resulting in 
weak core muscles.
Accelerated progression of scoliosis has never been 
associated with intrathecal baclofen initiation in an adult 
patient with SPS and is important to characterize because 
the cerebral palsy and SPS populations are fundamentally 
different.
4 Unlike cerebral palsy, SPS commonly presents in 
adulthood. A much larger proportion of patients with SPS 
have achieved skeletal maturity at the time of intrathecal 
baclofen initiation compared to patients with cerebral palsy, 
thus making it more difficult to induce scoliotic progres-
sion. In support of this, there is a paucity of reports of accel-
erated scoliosis in skeletally mature, adult patients while 
on intrathecal baclofen. Given skeletal immaturity, patients 
with cerebral palsy may require a smaller asymmetry in 
axial tone to accelerate scoliosis. Importantly, 2 case series 
involving patients with cerebral palsy and spastic quad-
riplegia on intrathecal baclofen recommend that patients 
should receive serial spine radiographs at regular intervals 
and receive early bracing and/or spinal fusion when scoli-
otic progression is >10° per year or when otherwise surgi-
cally indicated.
8,11 Similar parameters for intervention might 
be warranted in an adult population with scoliotic progres-
sion from intrathecal baclofen.
An inherent weakness of our case study is that, due 
to the complex nature of spine pathologies and interven-
tions, it is difficult to explain whether the patient’s pro-
gressive scoliosis is related to intrathecal baclofen or the 
natural history of her CIDP or SPS. However, it is more 
likely that this patient experienced accelerated progres-
sion of her underlying scoliotic curvature from intrathecal 
baclofen as opposed to the natural course of CIDP or SPS 
for several reasons. First, the scoliotic acceleration tempo-
rally correlates with intrathecal baclofen. The patient did 
not experience progression of her scoliotic curvature in 
the 4 years between initial SPS diagnosis and intrathecal 
treatment initiation. Second, CIDP results in flaccid paresis 
and paresthesias that commonly affect the distal extremi-
ties, not the axial muscles. On the other hand, SPS results 
in spasticity and increased tone, but not in asymmetric 
relaxation of axial muscles because it is a systemic process. 
Third, it is unlikely that either pathology led to scoliosis, as 
supported by a lack of reports on neuromuscular scoliosis 
and SPS or CIDP .
2,12 While SPS or CIDP alone do not cause 
scoliotic progression, it is likely that intrathecal baclofen 
in the setting of SPS and an underlying S-shaped scoliotic

curvature led to accelerated scoliotic progression in this 
patient.
Ultimately, this case report demonstrates the utility in 
being cautious when treating severe spasms and rigidity 
with intrathecal baclofen in adults with underlying scoliosis 
and SPS and/or other neuromuscular diseases that result 
in increased tone but underlying weakness. Further stud-
ies should validate and establish the prevalence of this phe-
nomenon, identify those at increased risk, and determine 
usefulness of close monitoring and early interventions for 
scoliotic acceleration in adult patients with SPS.
